## A New Question

<br>

So far — we've looked at data and [described]{.teal} what we saw

<br>

New question: [what mechanism could have *generated* this data?]{.gold}

<br>

::: {style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65); font-size: 0.85em;"}
*Probability is the language for describing that mechanism*
:::

---

## Why Probability?

<br>

Three questions probability helps us answer:

<br>

- [What outcomes are possible?]{.teal}
- [How likely is each outcome?]{.teal}
- [What changes if the process changes?]{.gold}

---

## Sample Space and Events

<br>

100 M&Ms in a jar:

| Blue | Red | Yellow |
|:----:|:---:|:------:|
| 45   | 40  | 15     |

<br>

- [**Sample space**]{.teal} — all possible outcomes: {Blue, Red, Yellow}
- [**Event**]{.teal} — any subset: {Blue, Yellow} = "not Red"
- [**Complement**]{.gold} — everything *except* the event: $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$

---

## One Draw

<br>

Two event examples:

- Event $A$: draw a <span style="color:#E85D5D; font-weight:600;">Red</span> M&M
- Event $B$: draw <span style="color:#5BC8DB; font-weight:600;">Blue</span> or <span style="color:#F6D743; font-weight:600;">Yellow</span>

<br>

```{=html}
<div style="font-size: 1.05em; line-height: 1.6; margin-top: 0.2em;">
  <div>P(A) = P(Red) = 0.40</div>
  <div>P(B) = P(Blue or Yellow) = 0.45 + 0.15 = 0.60</div>
</div>
```

---

## Two Draws: Does the Process Change?

<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[With replacement]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"}

Put the M&M back before drawing again

→ jar is the same each time

→ draws are [**independent**]{.gold}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Without replacement]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"}

Don't put it back

→ jar changes after the first draw

→ draws are [**not independent**]{.gold}
:::
::::

<br>

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
The mechanism you choose changes the probability
:::

---

## Independence

<br>

[Key question:]{.gold style="font-weight: 600;"} Does knowing the first outcome change the probability of the second?

<br>

- Yes → [**dependent**]{.teal}
- No → [**independent**]{.teal}

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
Independent ≠ mutually exclusive — these are *different* ideas
:::

---

## Probability as a Polling Model

<br>

Suppose a congressional district has:

| <span style="color:#5BC8DB; font-weight:600;">Democrats</span> | <span style="color:#E85D5D; font-weight:600;">Republicans</span> | <span style="color:#F6D743; font-weight:600;">Neither</span> |
|:---------:|:-----------:|:-------:|
| <span style="color:#5BC8DB; font-weight:600;">45%</span> | <span style="color:#E85D5D; font-weight:600;">40%</span> | <span style="color:#F6D743; font-weight:600;">15%</span> |

<br>

Loading an M&M jar with [these proportions]{.gold} models a phone poll

→ one draw = one randomly contacted voter

---

## Sample Variability

<br>

If we call 100 voters — do we expect [exactly]{.teal} 45 to be Democrats?

<br>

[No.]{.gold style="font-size: 1.1em;"} We expect *close to* 45 — but not exactly

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
This is sample variability — it's expected, not an error in the model
:::

---

## Bias Enters Through the Process

<br>

What if Democrats are less likely to answer the phone?

<br>

Then the M&M jar model is wrong — not because of variability, but because the [mechanism itself is flawed]{.gold}

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
This is nonresponse bias — a problem with how data are generated
:::

---

## Union and Intersection

<br>

70% use Spotify · 15% use Apple Music

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em; line-height: 1.55;"}
General rule:
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$

No overlap:
$0.70 + 0.15 = 0.85$

10% overlap:
$0.70 + 0.15 - 0.10 = 0.75$
:::

<br>

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
*(Venn diagram on board)*
:::

---

## "At Least One" and the Complement

<br>

Two ways to get the same answer:

<br>

[Union (direct):]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"} $P(A \cup B) = 0.70 + 0.15 - 0.10 = 0.75$

[Complement (shortcut):]{.gold style="font-weight: 600;"} $1 - P(\text{neither}) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75$

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
Use the complement when *P(none)* is easier to compute than *P(at least one)* — e.g. independent events: $(1-p_1)(1-p_2)\cdots$
:::

---

## What Conditioning Means

<br>

$P(A \mid B)$ = probability of $A$, given that [$B$ is already known]{.gold}

<br>

- Conditioning narrows the sample space to outcomes [where $B$ is true]{.teal}
- If $B$ is relevant to $A$ → probability changes
- If $B$ is irrelevant to $A$ → probability stays the same

---

## Conditional Probability

<br>

Wildfire risk $W$ in the Santa Cruz mountains (0–100) · Humidity $X$ known

$X$ and $W$ have a [negative relationship]{.teal}

<br>

- Definition: $P(A \mid B)$ means probability of $A$ once $B$ is known
- Compare: $P(W > 80 \mid X = 30\%)$ vs $P(W > 80 \mid X = 70\%)$

<br>

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
*The condition tells us something relevant — so the probability shifts*
:::

## Recurring Patterns

<br>

Some random mechanisms appear over and over in nature

→ statisticians give them names: [**probability distributions**]{.gold}

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
A distribution is a model for a generating process
:::

---

## Variable Types

<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Discrete]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"}

Takes whole number values

- number of heads in 10 flips
- number of Democrats called

Distribution example from lecture:

<span style="color:#E5A823; font-weight:600;">Binomial</span> (count of successes in $n$ trials)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Continuous]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"}

Can take any value

- height, weight, temperature
- wildfire risk score

Distribution example from lecture:

<span style="color:#E5A823; font-weight:600;">Normal</span> (SAT/IQ-style bell-shaped measurements)
:::
::::

---

## A Familiar Shape

<br>

Many natural measurements cluster near a typical value — with fewer extremes

<br>

```{=html}
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center; margin-top: 0.6em; margin-bottom: 0.6em;">
  <svg width="720" height="220" viewBox="0 0 720 220" role="img" aria-label="Normal distribution curve with mean and standard deviation markers">
    <line x1="60" y1="180" x2="660" y2="180" stroke="rgba(255,255,255,0.55)" stroke-width="2"></line>
    <path d="M90,180 C180,180 220,45 360,45 C500,45 540,180 630,180" fill="none" stroke="#5BC8DB" stroke-width="4"></path>
    <line x1="360" y1="180" x2="360" y2="52" stroke="#E5A823" stroke-width="2.5"></line>
    <line x1="270" y1="180" x2="270" y2="102" stroke="rgba(255,255,255,0.45)" stroke-width="2"></line>
    <line x1="450" y1="180" x2="450" y2="102" stroke="rgba(255,255,255,0.45)" stroke-width="2"></line>
    <text x="360" y="198" fill="#E5A823" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15">mean</text>
    <text x="270" y="198" fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.75)" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">-1 SD</text>
    <text x="450" y="198" fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.75)" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14">+1 SD</text>
  </svg>
</div>
```

<br>

- [68%]{.gold} of values fall within 1 SD of the mean
- [95%]{.gold} within 2 SDs · [99.7%]{.gold} within 3 SDs

## Regression as an EDA Tool

<br>

We haven't covered regression in section yet — here's the key idea:

<br>

[Regression describes a linear pattern in the data]{.gold}

<br>

- [Slope:]{.teal} for 1-unit increase in x, y changes by ___ *on average*
- [Intercept:]{.teal} predicted y when x = 0 *(ask: is x = 0 realistic here?)*
- [R²:]{.teal} proportion of variation in y explained by x

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.6);"}
*Description, not causation*
:::

---

## Tips: Problems 2–3

<br>

- [Explanatory → x-axis]{.teal} · Response → y-axis
- [Residual]{.teal} = actual − predicted *(order matters)*
- High R² ≠ causation — it just means the linear fit is good
- Check the intercept: does x = 0 make sense in this context?

<br>

[Google Sheets:]{.gold} `=SLOPE(y_range, x_range)` &nbsp; `=INTERCEPT(y_range, x_range)`
